solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One very quietly performing gets ten points

definitions.note: a judo term for a winning score worth ten points

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
pianissimo, the musical marking for very quiet
an actor who is performing is on

explanation.surface: A performer playing very softly earns a perfect score from the judges.
explanation.definitionFit: In judo an ippon is the decisive full point, historically scored as ten points, which wins the bout outright.

clue.text: Bard's wink, inserting extra line into epic poem

indicators.note: inserting means one item is pushed inside another, here the extra letter goes inside the poem

blocks.note: Homer's epic of the Trojan War
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Shakespeare winks while slipping an extra line into the Iliad.
explanation.walkthrough: ILIAD with a second L added gives ILLIAD, Shakespeare's word for a flirtatious glance.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiad is Shakespeare's anglicised form of the French oeillade, an amorous ogle, so 'Bard's' flags his usage.

clue.text: Charge servant to capture dog when breaking free of lead

indicators.note: to capture something is to hold it inside, so one piece surrounds the other
breaking free of the lead means losing the leading letter of the word

blocks.note: a page is a young servant
a hound is a hunting dog

explanation.surface: A servant is told to catch a dog that has slipped its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface 'lead' is a dog's leash; cryptically it is the first letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Poundage is a charge or fee levied at so much per pound, in weight or money.

clue.text: Physical training involving reprimand or approval

indicators.note: something involving another item takes it in, so these letters wrap round the other word

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for physical training
to lace, as in lace into, is to thrash or scold

explanation.surface: A PE lesson ends in either a telling-off or a word of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: LACE sits between P and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A placet is a formal vote of assent, from the Latin 'it pleases', used in university and church assemblies.

clue.text: Chemical engineers needing some information first

blocks.note: a nit (or nepit) is a unit of information, like a bit
the Royal Engineers

explanation.surface: Chemical engineers want some data before they start work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' tells you the information unit goes before the engineers. A nit is a natural-logarithm unit of information, a little-known sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre is potassium nitrate, saltpetre, a chemical compound used in gunpowder and fertiliser.

clue.text: Grey-haired Greek has died on Tinos maybe

blocks.note: GR is the abbreviation for Greek
Tinos is a Greek island, an example of an isle
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: An old grey Greek man has died on his island home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'died on Tinos maybe' puts D after ISLE, as across clues read 'on' as 'following'.
explanation.definitionFit: Grisled is a variant of grizzled, meaning streaked with grey, used of hair or of an old person.

clue.text: Impression created by deadly place outside old city

indicators.note: a word placed outside another surrounds it on both sides

blocks.note: a grave is where the dead lie
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, the crossword's favourite old city

explanation.surface: A sombre impression is left by a burial ground beyond an ancient city's walls.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravure is a print made by photogravure, an impression taken from an engraved plate.

clue.text: Renounce Irish booze with little hesitation after upset

indicators.note: in a down clue something upset is turned upside down, so the letters are read from the bottom

blocks.note: gin is a common spirit
er is the short sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: Someone stammers as they give up drinking spirits in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: GIN then ER, all reversed. 'Irish' is padding for the surface rather than part of the wordplay; there is no IR in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Renig is a variant spelling of renege, to go back on a promise or give something up.

clue.text: Tragic girl brought up to keep still shows a range of aptitudes

indicators.note: in a down clue bringing something up lifts it bottom to top, so the name is read backwards
to keep something is to hold it inside, so the name surrounds the other word

blocks.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Hardy's tragic heroine
to kill a sound or a breeze is to still it

explanation.surface: A doomed girl who learns to keep still turns out to be talented.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed name splits after its first letter to take in the verb; to kill a breeze or a noise is an old way of saying to still it.
explanation.definitionFit: A skill set is the collection of abilities a person has, so it is a range of aptitudes.

clue.text: Whale in group to go wild

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the sei is a species of rorqual whale
a lot is a group or batch

explanation.surface: A whale caught up in a pod starts to thrash about wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: The sei is a crossword regular among whales, along with the orc.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose it is the idiom for losing self-control, flying into a rage or panic.

clue.text: Fourth character, one chattering a lot in film

blocks.note: D is the fourth letter of the alphabet, spelt out as dee
a pie is a magpie, a famously noisy bird

explanation.surface: The fourth character in a film is a chatterbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' in the surface sounds like a role; here it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A deepie is an old informal name for a three-dimensional film, coined as a pun on talkie and movie.

clue.text: Flashily dressed idler, a drunk

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so these letters are tumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gaudily dressed layabout is drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang a lair is a show-off, and to be laired up is to be dressed flashily.

clue.text: Last bit of black mineral used for statue

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter only

blocks.note: the final letter of black
ore is mineral rock from which metal is extracted

explanation.surface: The final scrap of a dark mineral is used to carve a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: A kore is an archaic Greek sculpture of a standing young woman, a type of statue.

clue.text: Fortune not half needed to get gold dish

indicators.note: not half means only half the word survives, the rest being dropped

blocks.note: luck is fortune
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A half-share of a fortune is needed to buy a golden plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A luau is a Hawaiian feast, and also a dish of taro leaves cooked with coconut and meat.

clue.text: Second in cabinet in state abroad?

definitions.text: Second in cabinet in state abroad

indicators.note: the second of a word is the letter in position two
abroad suggests being scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

blocks.note: the second letter of cabinet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Who is deputy leader of the government in another country?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while its words also build it: the second letter of cabinet plus IN STATE, rearranged. The Tanaiste is Ireland's deputy prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tanaiste is Ireland's deputy head of government, literally second in the Irish cabinet, a state abroad from a British view.

clue.text: Plant in vehicle? Very bad — needing water

blocks.note: in, plus car for a vehicle
V is the abbreviation for very
ill means bad, as in ill luck
ea is a dialect word for a river or stream

explanation.surface: A plant left in the car is in very poor shape and needs watering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb for hiding something in the car; it is the definition. EA, a Northern dialect word for a river, is a staple of barred crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Incarvillea is a genus of perennial flowering plants from Asia, sometimes called hardy gloxinia.

clue.text: Nomadic people on journeys — they make music

blocks.note: the San are hunter-gatherer people of southern Africa
tours are journeys

explanation.surface: Wandering tribes on the road are travelling musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Santours are Persian hammered dulcimers, stringed instruments that produce music when struck.

clue.text: Provide excuse for a sexual impulse — finish being banned

indicators.note: something banned is excluded, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
libido is sexual drive
to do is to finish, as in 'that's done it'

explanation.surface: Someone tries to excuse a sexual urge by saying it's all over now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provide excuse for' is a verb phrase, so the answer is the verb sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Alibi as a verb means to supply someone with an alibi, an account that excuses them.

clue.text: Straitlaced person used a hankie, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear points to what is heard rather than written

blocks.note: using a handkerchief means you blew your nose

explanation.surface: A prudish person discreetly dabs at their nose with a handkerchief.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluenose is American slang for a puritanical, prudish person who disapproves of others' pleasures.

clue.text: Short play about a label used for information packet

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the last letter is dropped
about means surrounding, so one part goes round the other

blocks.note: a drama is a play
taken as written
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: A brief play about a label is used to carry information.
explanation.definitionFit: A datagram is a self-contained unit of data sent across a network, a packet of information.

clue.text: What's endlessly mysterious about the chap from a bygone age

indicators.note: endlessly means without an ending, so the last letter is dropped
about means surrounding, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: arcane means secret or mysterious
he refers to a chap

explanation.surface: Something endlessly puzzling about a man from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's' simply joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Archean (Archaean) refers to the geological eon over 2.5 billion years ago, so belonging to a very ancient era.

clue.text: Second bomb came out of nowhere?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
prang is old RAF slang for a bombing raid, or to bomb

explanation.surface: A second bomb appeared out of nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: something that sprang up came out of nowhere. Prang is British slang for a crash or a bombing raid.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprang is the past tense of spring, and springing up is appearing suddenly, as if from nowhere.

clue.text: Let's have more Italian stories to entertain a hundred soldiers!

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so these letters hold the others

blocks.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or table talk
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: An audience of soldiers calls out for more Italian tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian' marks the answer as an Italian word. Ana, a collection of sayings, and OR for other ranks are crossword staples.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancora is the Italian cry of encore, an audience demanding a repeat performance.

clue.text: Dog running around in certain British sports field

indicators.note: running around suggests turning to face the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: sure means certain
B is the abbreviation for British
a rec is a recreation ground, a public playing field

explanation.surface: A dog chases about a British sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: SURE, B and REC are joined and the whole read backwards. In British usage the rec is the local recreation ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the underworld in Greek myth.

clue.text: One criticising short film — waste of time

indicators.note: a waste of something means it is thrown away, so that letter is lost

blocks.note: a trailer is a short preview film
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A critic calls a short film a waste of time.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAILER without T.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail is to complain bitterly, so a railer is a person who scolds or criticises.

clue.text: Very wet piece of turf in which bomb has turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue turning something up flips it bottom to top, so it reads backwards
in which places the next item inside the one just named

blocks.note: a sod is a piece of turf
egg is old military slang for a bomb

explanation.surface: A bomb has turned up in a sodden piece of lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Egg for a bomb is old wartime slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Sogged is an older form of soggy, meaning soaked through with water.

clue.text: Coverings in shed — put first one at back

indicators.note: the opening letter is moved from the front to the end

blocks.note: shed as a past participle, cast off or used up

explanation.surface: Covers inside a garden shed are shuffled from the front to the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: SPENT has its S moved to the end. 'Shed' looks like a noun, a garden building; it is a verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: A pent is a penthouse in the old sense, a sloping lean-to roof, so pents are protective coverings.

clue.text: In Ayr aim to make permanent home, having abandoned south

indicators.note: having abandoned something means leaving it out

blocks.note: to settle is to make a permanent home
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A Scot in Ayr plans to settle down for good, having left the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Ayr' marks a Scots word; Ayr is a town in south-west Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ettle is a Scots verb meaning to intend or aim, still found in Burns country.

clue.text: Married man losing heart inclined to get stuck in?

indicators.note: losing heart means dropping the central letter of a word

blocks.note: wed means married
a guy is a man

explanation.surface: A husband who has lost his spirit wonders whether to get stuck in.
explanation.walkthrough: GUY loses its middle letter. The question mark covers a playful definition: a wedge is driven in and sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: Wedgy means wedge-like, and a wedge is something designed to be jammed tight into a gap.

clue.text: Burning boat seen at start of operatic cycle

blocks.note: a scow is a flat-bottomed barge
The Ring, Wagner's cycle of four operas

explanation.surface: A boat goes up in flames at the opening of Wagner's operas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen at start of' puts the boat before the cycle.
explanation.definitionFit: Scowther is a Scots verb meaning to scorch or singe, so scowthering means burning.

clue.text: Donate millions, university being broke? It's added up

indicators.note: something broke is broken, so the letters are smashed and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for millions
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Will a cash-strapped university add up the millions it needs to be given?
explanation.definitionFit: To amount to is to total or sum, so something that amounted has been totalled up.

clue.text: Strike a setback for activity involving clubs

indicators.note: a setback sets something back, so the word runs in the opposite direction

blocks.note: golf is played with clubs

explanation.surface: A walkout at the golf club is a setback.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog is to beat or whip, so it means to strike repeatedly.

clue.text: Race back to river in bit of wood — hard

indicators.note: back tells you to read the word in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a run is a race
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A boat races back to the river, with a hard lump of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: RUN reversed, then R.
explanation.definitionFit: A nurr (knur) is a hard knot in a tree trunk, a tough lump of wood.

clue.text: What you completely see with no clouds having a silver lining? Nonsense!

indicators.note: having something as a lining means it is held inside

blocks.clueFragment: What you completely see with no clouds
blocks.note: a cloudless sky is all blue
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver; a lining goes inside

explanation.surface: Every cloud has a silver lining? A clear sky makes nonsense of that.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on the proverb about clouds and silver linings; 'lining' tells you the metal goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Blague is a French-derived word for humbug, bluster or claptrap, so it serves as an exclamation of nonsense.

clue.text: Girl grabbed by dope — easily seen through as before?

indicators.note: something grabbed by another is held within its grasp

blocks.note: dope and gen are both slang for information
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A naive girl is taken in by a dope dealer whose lies are transparent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' looks like a drug or a fool, but here it means information. 'As before' marks an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Glassen is an obsolete adjective meaning made of glass, and glass is transparent.

clue.text: You had to get doctor in — feared no longer

indicators.note: getting someone in means bringing them inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: ye'd is an old contraction of ye had
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: You had to call the doctor in, but the fear has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ye'd is an old contraction of 'ye had'. 'No longer' marks an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ydred is Spenser's archaic past participle of dread, so it means dreaded or feared in old usage.
